subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Defining the Nudge
description: A short lesson to help you apply Defining the Nudge.

hook.text: A fly sticker inside a urinal reduced bathroom spillage by 80%. Nobody was forced. Nobody was told. That's a nudge.

buildup.text: Thaler and Sunstein define a nudge as any part of choice design that shifts behavior without banning options.

discovery.text: A nudge alters how choices are presented, not what choices exist. You're free to ignore it. Most people don't.

twist.text: Banning junk food isn't a nudge. Putting fruit at eye level is. The distinction is freedom. Nudges always preserve it.

climax.text: Nudges work because humans take shortcuts. The architect of the shortcut shapes the outcome.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a nudge from a mandate?
options: A nudge changes behavior while preserving freedom of choice
A nudge always costs money to implement

details.summary: A nudge is any aspect of choice architecture that predictably alters behavior without forbidding options or significantly changing economic incentives. Nudges steer decisions while preserving freedom of choice, making the preferred option easier but the alternatives still available.
details.whyItMatters: The definition of a nudge matters because it determines the boundary between acceptable influence and manipulation. True nudges preserve choice, are transparent, and aim to benefit the chooser.
takeaways: Nudges alter behavior without removing options or changing economic incentives
The choice architecture is never neutral, so defaults are always nudging someone
Libertarian paternalism guides choices while preserving freedom to choose otherwise

faq.question: What makes a nudge different from a mandate or a ban?
faq.answer: A mandate requires the behavior and a ban prohibits it. A nudge makes one option easier or more salient without restricting alternatives. Placing healthy food at eye level is a nudge. Banning junk food is a mandate. Both reduce junk food consumption but through different mechanisms.

faq.question: Is it possible to have a choice architecture that does not nudge?
faq.answer: No. Any arrangement of options influences choice. The order items appear, which option is default, and how information is presented all nudge toward certain choices. There is no neutral design. The question is not whether to nudge but which direction to nudge.
